title: Animal Body Plans: Similar Bodies, Different Branches

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Which five features make up an animal's body plan?
cards.back: Its symmetry, tissue layers, body cavity, gut and embryonic development: the basic layout it shares with its relatives.
cards.quote: A body plan is the basic layout an animal shares with its relatives: its symmetry, tissue layers, body cavity, gut and embryonic development.
cards.section: Characters you can see: symmetry, layers, cavities

cards.front: How does bilateral symmetry differ from radial symmetry?
cards.back: Radial: parts arranged around a central axis, so several cuts through it give similar halves. Bilateral: only one plane gives left and right halves, usually with a front end where sense organs cluster.
cards.quote: Bilateral symmetry allows only one plane that divides the body into roughly equivalent left and right halves, usually with a front end where sense organs cluster.
cards.section: Characters you can see: symmetry, layers, cavities

cards.front: What separates a diploblastic animal from a triploblastic one?
cards.back: Diploblastic: two germ layers, outer ectoderm and inner endoderm. Triploblastic: adds a middle mesoderm, which forms muscle and much of the body wall.
cards.quote: A diploblastic animal has two, an outer ectoderm and an inner endoderm.
cards.section: Characters you can see: symmetry, layers, cavities

cards.front: A true coelom is a fluid-filled body cavity lined {{c1::entirely by mesoderm}}.
cards.back: A pseudocoelom lacks a complete mesodermal lining around the gut; in an acoelomate, tissue fills the region between gut and body wall.
cards.quote: a coelom is a fluid-filled body cavity lined entirely by mesoderm
cards.section: Characters you can see: symmetry, layers, cavities

cards.front: A planarian flatworm is called acoelomate, yet it has a gut. Why is there no contradiction?
cards.back: The body cavity is not the gut lumen, where food goes. Acoelomate means tissue fills the region between gut and body wall; the gut is still there.
cards.quote: None is the gut lumen, where food goes: an acoelomate planarian still has a gut.
cards.section: Characters you can see: symmetry, layers, cavities

cards.front: A specimen is bilateral and triploblastic, with a fluid-filled cavity lined entirely by mesoderm and a gut running from mouth to anus. Describe its body plan, and say whether that description places it in Spiralia.
cards.back: A bilateral, triploblastic coelomate with a through gut, like the earthworm Lumbricus terrestris. The description alone does not place it: coelomates occur in Spiralia, Ecdysozoa and Deuterostomia.
cards.why: Body-plan characters describe an animal; its branch needs a tree built from other evidence.
cards.quote: the earthworm Lumbricus terrestris (coelom) each have a through gut, from mouth to anus
cards.section: Characters you can see: symmetry, layers, cavities

cards.front: What is the difference between a grade and a clade?
cards.back: A grade is a set of animals that share a level of organization. A clade is an ancestor and all of its descendants.
cards.quote: a grade, animals that share a level of organization, and set it against a clade, an ancestor and all of its descendants

cards.front: What is a shared derived character, and why can it mark a clade?
cards.back: A new state that arose in a common ancestor and passed to its descendants, so animals sharing it share that ancestor. Example: the moulted cuticle marks Ecdysozoa.
cards.quote: A shared, derived character, a new state that arose in a common ancestor and passed to its descendants, can mark a clade, as the moulted cuticle does.

cards.front: Why can a missing coelom not mark a clade by itself?
cards.back: The absence may be the ancestral state, or the same loss may have happened more than once, so animals lacking a coelom need not share one ancestor.
cards.quote: the absence may be the ancestral state, or the same loss may have happened more than once.

cards.front: A lineage descended from segmented annelid ancestors has lost its segments. Is it still an annelid?
cards.back: Yes. Clade membership follows descent, not the current state of a character; a few descendants may later lose a shared derived character.
cards.quote: A few descendants may later lose it; annelids that have lost their segments are still annelids.

cards.front: How can you tell whether a body-plan character arose only once?
cards.back: Build the tree from other evidence (many anatomical characters, many genes or chromosome linkage), then lay the character on it and count the changes it needs.
cards.quote: Build the tree from other evidence (many other anatomical characters, many genes or chromosome linkage), then lay the character on it.

cards.front: Comparisons of 18S ribosomal RNA genes, later broadly supported by many-gene analyses, regrouped which worms, and what does that show about body plans?
cards.back: Nematodes went with arthropods and other moulting animals, not with annelids, and flatworms fell inside Spiralia. Similar worm-shaped body plans need not mark a clade.
cards.quote: compared 18S ribosomal RNA genes and grouped nematodes with arthropods and other moulting animals, not with annelids

cards.front: Coded on the gene tree for eight phyla, body cavity needs 3 changes (minimum on any tree 2), segments 3 (minimum 1) and the moulted cuticle 1 (minimum 1). Interpret each.
cards.back: Body-cavity groups are grades, and segmented animals do not form a clade. The moulted cuticle fits a single origin that marks Ecdysozoa, named after ecdysis, moulting of a cuticle.
cards.why: A character that needs extra changes on a tree built from other evidence arose or was lost more than once.
cards.quote: On the gene tree, body cavity needs one change more than any tree must, segments need three where one would do, and the moulted cuticle needs only one.

cards.front: Why did Hyman's staircase of body cavities look right to zoologists?
cards.back: Built from cavity type, it needs only two cavity changes, the fewest possible. Testing the character needs a tree built from other evidence.
cards.quote: built from cavity type, it needs only two cavity changes, the fewest possible.

cards.front: Segments need three changes on the gene tree. Why does that not prove segmentation arose three times?
cards.back: Three changes could be three origins, or one origin and later losses. The count is a worked count on a coarse coding, not a history.
cards.quote: three segment changes could be three origins or one origin and later losses

cards.front: Name the four animal groups that sit outside Bilateria.
cards.back: Sponges, comb jellies, placozoans and cnidarians. Which of these split off first is unsettled.
cards.quote: sit sponges, comb jellies, placozoans and cnidarians; which of these split off first is unsettled

cards.front: Into which two clades does Protostomia split, and which phyla fall in each?
cards.back: Spiralia: flatworms, annelids, molluscs, nemerteans and rotifers. Ecdysozoa: nematodes and arthropods. Deuterostomia (echinoderms, hemichordates, chordates) is the traditional third group, with equivocal support in one recent analysis.
cards.quote: Inside, Protostomia splits into Spiralia (flatworms, annelids, molluscs, nemerteans and rotifers) and Ecdysozoa (nematodes and arthropods).

cards.front: Why is it wrong to call sponges or cnidarians the ancestors of bilaterians?
cards.back: No living phylum is an ancestor of another. Sponges and cnidarians are branches with as long a history as ours, not steps on a ladder.
cards.quote: No living phylum is an ancestor of another: sponges and cnidarians are branches with as long a history as ours, not steps on a ladder.

cards.front: An adult sea star is radial, like a jellyfish. Does it belong with the cnidarians or inside Bilateria, and what explains its shape?
cards.back: Inside Bilateria, placed there by trees built from many anatomical and molecular characters. Its larva is bilateral; the five-part radial adult develops later, a change within a bilaterian lineage.
cards.quote: The larva then explains the shape: it is bilateral, and the five-part radial adult develops from it later, a change within a bilaterian lineage.

cards.front: What is the blastopore, and what does it become in protostomes and in deuterostomes?
cards.back: The opening connecting the forming gut to the outside during gastrulation. Protostomes: it becomes the mouth. Deuterostomes: the mouth forms separately, and the blastopore often becomes the anus.
cards.quote: In deuterostomes ("mouth second") the mouth forms separately, and the blastopore often becomes the anus.
cards.section: Testing an old rule: the blastopore

cards.front: How does spiral cleavage differ from radial cleavage, and which animals show each?
cards.back: Spiral: early divisions in a tilted pattern (many annelids, molluscs and other spiralians). Radial: cells stacked directly above one another (echinoderms and many other deuterostomes).
cards.quote: echinoderms and many other deuterostomes divide in a radial pattern, with cells stacked directly above one another
cards.section: Testing an old rule: the blastopore

cards.front: Fate mapping with labelled cells in the slipper snail Crepidula fornicata, a spiralian, followed the blastopore and the anus. What did each come from?
cards.back: The blastopore became the mouth, as the protostome rule predicts. The anus formed separately and late, at about 12 days, from descendants of the 2d2 cell, not from the classic "anal cells".
cards.quote: The anus formed separately and late, at about 12 days of development, from descendants of the 2d2 cell.
cards.section: Testing an old rule: the blastopore

cards.front: In the slipper snail Crepidula fornicata the blastopore becomes the mouth. Does this confirm blastopore fate as a test of the major bilaterian clades?
cards.back: No. One species is not a clade test: blastopore fate varies even among close relatives, and the study's authors note it is not a reliable test of the major clades.
cards.quote: One species is not a clade test: blastopore fate varies even among close relatives
cards.section: Testing an old rule: the blastopore

cards.front: Which phylum is characterised by a mantle, and what is a mantle?
cards.back: Mollusca. The mantle is a fold of tissue over the visceral mass (the soft body holding most organs); in many species it secretes a shell.
cards.quote: Mollusca: a mantle, a fold of tissue over the visceral mass (the soft body that holds most organs), which in many species secretes a shell.

cards.front: What feature defines Chordata?
cards.back: A notochord, a flexible rod along the back, present during at least part of development.
cards.quote: Chordata: a notochord, a flexible rod along the back, during at least part of development

cards.front: Nematodes and arthropods look very different. Which feature do they share, and which features separate them?
cards.back: Both moult a cuticle, marking Ecdysozoa. Nematodes are unsegmented roundworms with a pseudocoelom; arthropods have jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton.
cards.quote: Arthropoda: jointed appendages and a chitinous exoskeleton that is moulted.

cards.front: A collected worm is unsegmented, has a fluid-filled cavity lacking a complete mesodermal lining around the gut, and sheds its cuticle as it grows. Name its phylum and its major clade.
cards.back: Nematoda, a roundworm with a pseudocoelom and a moulted cuticle. The moulted cuticle places it in Ecdysozoa, within Protostomia.
cards.quote: Nematoda: unsegmented roundworms with a pseudocoelom and a cuticle that is moulted.

cards.front: In the earthworm Lumbricus terrestris, what forms the hydrostatic skeleton, and what lets each segment act largely on its own?
cards.back: Incompressible coelomic fluid held in by the muscular body wall. Septa largely partition it, so in textbook accounts each segment acts as a largely independent hydraulic unit.
cards.quote: septa largely partition it, and in textbook accounts each segment acts as a largely independent hydraulic unit
cards.section: What a coelom, a through gut and segments allow

cards.front: Why is a sealed, constant-volume segment only a model of a real earthworm segment?
cards.back: The septa are not perfect seals: the gut runs through them.
cards.quote: The septa are not perfect seals (the gut runs through them), so a sealed, constant-volume segment is a model.
cards.section: What a coelom, a through gut and segments allow

cards.front: Besides acting as a hydrostatic skeleton, what does the coelom allow the gut and other organs to do?
cards.back: Grow and move with some independence from the body wall, within the limits of their attachments.
cards.quote: The coelom also lets the gut and other organs grow and move with some independence from the body wall
cards.section: What a coelom, a through gut and segments allow

cards.front: Circular muscles halve the diameter of a sealed, constant-volume worm segment. Is it now twice as long, or more?
cards.back: Four times as long. Volume is cross-section times length; cross-section scales with radius squared, so halving the diameter cuts it to a quarter and length rises four-fold.
cards.quote: halve the diameter and it falls to a quarter, so the length rises four-fold
cards.section: What a coelom, a through gut and segments allow

cards.front: A worm segment, modelled as a sealed cylinder of incompressible fluid, is 5.0 mm in diameter and 4.0 mm long. Circular muscles narrow it to 4.0 mm in diameter. What is its new length?
cards.back: Length scales with (old diameter / new diameter)^2 at constant volume: 4.0 mm x (5.0/4.0)^2 = 4.0 x 1.5625 = 6.25 mm, about 6.3 mm.
cards.quote: 1.78 times as long, which is (4/3)^2: narrowing by 4/3 lengthens by its square.
cards.section: What a coelom, a through gut and segments allow

cards.front: A sealed, constant-volume worm segment is 4.0 mm in diameter and 4.0 mm long. Longitudinal muscles shorten it to 2.0 mm. What is its new diameter?
cards.back: Halving the length doubles the cross-section, so r^2 doubles and diameter rises by the square root of 2: 4.0 mm x 1.414 = about 5.7 mm.
cards.quote: Reverse: longitudinal muscles shorten it to 1.5 mm
cards.section: What a coelom, a through gut and segments allow

cards.front: A sealed, constant-volume worm segment 4.0 mm in diameter must lengthen 1.5-fold. To what diameter must circular muscles narrow it?
cards.back: Cross-section must fall to 1/1.5 of its start, so diameter falls by 1/sqrt(1.5) = 0.816: 4.0 mm x 0.816 = about 3.3 mm.
cards.quote: Volume is cross-section times length, and the cross-section goes with the radius squared
cards.section: What a coelom, a through gut and segments allow

cards.front: A nematode such as C. elegans is a fluid-filled tube with one shared pseudocoelom and no circular muscle. Can it crawl by lengthening one region at a time, as an earthworm does?
cards.back: No. A squeeze anywhere raises pressure along the whole cavity, so no region lengthens on its own, and no circular muscle can narrow one. It bends instead, using longitudinal muscles against its pressurized body and cuticle.
cards.quote: A squeeze anywhere raises pressure along the whole cavity, so no compartment can lengthen on its own the way an earthworm segment does
cards.section: What a coelom, a through gut and segments allow

cards.front: Older schemes grouped segmented annelids and arthropods as the Articulata. Gene trees instead group unsegmented, pseudocoelomate nematodes with arthropods. If the gene tree is right, what histories of segmentation are possible, and what follows for groups built on segments or cavity type?
cards.back: Segmentation arose more than once, or was present in a common ancestor and lost in many lineages (still debated). The nematode pseudocoelom could likewise be a change from a coelomate ancestor. Either way, such groups are grades, not clades.
cards.quote: segmentation either arose more than once (in annelids and in arthropods) or was present in a common ancestor and lost in many lineages

cards.front: A single-gene tree groups nematodes with arthropods, against traditional schemes. Design a test of whether Ecdysozoa is real.
cards.back: Sample hundreds of genes from many species, with models that allow for uneven rates of change, and add a different kind of evidence, such as which genes share chromosomes. If the sources agree, keep Ecdysozoa.
cards.why: A single gene can mislead when some lineages' sequences change fast.
cards.quote: sample hundreds of genes from many species with models that allow for uneven rates, and add a different kind of evidence

cards.front: Which ways of forming the coelom do textbooks pair with protostomes and with deuterostomes?
cards.back: Protostomes: schizocoely, a coelom opening within masses of mesoderm. Deuterostomes: enterocoely, pouches budding off the gut wall.
cards.quote: Textbooks also pair protostomes with schizocoely, a coelom opening within masses of mesoderm, and deuterostomes with enterocoely, pouches budding off the gut wall.

cards.front: In chromosome-linkage studies of early animal branches, why does a shared fused, intermixed state of two gene sets mark shared ancestry?
cards.back: Gene sets that fuse and then mix are very unlikely to separate again, so lineages sharing the state inherited it. This evidence supports comb jellies as sister to all other animals, one line among several.
cards.quote: gene sets that fuse and then mix are very unlikely to separate again, so a shared fused, mixed state marks shared ancestry
cards.section: The deepest branches: sponges or comb jellies?

cards.front: Flatworms are acoelomate, yet they sit in Spiralia among coelomate annelids and molluscs. What two readings of their acoelomate body does this allow?
cards.back: It may be a secondary simplification from a coelomate ancestor. But some analyses suggest the first spiralians had no coelom, so it could be ancestral; the ancestral bilaterian state is still debated.
cards.why: An absent character can be the ancestral state or a loss; only its position on the tree weighs the two.
cards.quote: Because flatworms sit among coelomate relatives, their acoelomate body may well be a secondary simplification.

cards.front: The sea anemone Nematostella vectensis has a second body axis at right angles to its mouth-to-foot axis, patterned by Chordin and BMP. Why does this not settle whether bilateral symmetry has a single origin?
cards.back: The axis could share an origin with the bilaterian axis, or have arisen by convergence; the question is still open.
cards.why: A similar state can arise twice, so resemblance alone does not show a single origin.
cards.quote: Whether that axis means bilaterality has one origin or arose by convergence is still open.
cards.section: A second axis in a sea anemone

cards.front: A many-gene analysis places a hypothetical pseudocoelomate worm phylum inside Spiralia, far from nematodes. Does this contradict Ecdysozoa?
cards.back: No. A pseudocoelom is a grade character that can arise or be lost more than once; Ecdysozoa rests on the moulted cuticle and many-gene trees, not on cavity type.
cards.why: Body-cavity groups are grades; a shared derived character tested on a tree marks the clade.
cards.quote: So the body-cavity groups are grades, the segmented animals do not form a clade
